reason: The sources provide over 15 consistent claims from multiple contemporary and scientific perspectives, supporting a dramatic 45-second story about a landlocked Alpine tsunami.
story: In 563 AD, a mountain known as Tauredunum collapsed at the eastern end of Lake Geneva. Contemporary chroniclers Gregory of Tours and Marius of Avenches recorded a disaster that modern science has only recently confirmed: a massive tsunami in the heart of the Alps. The mountainside collapse struck the Rhone delta with such force that it triggered a massive underwater mudslide, displacing millions of cubic meters of sediment. This displacement created a wave that raced across the lake at 45 miles per hour. It struck Lausanne in just 15 minutes, standing over 40 feet high. Within 70 minutes, the wave reached Geneva, miles from the impact site. The wall of water demolished the city's bridge and mills before surging over the high city walls, drowning inhabitants inside. Today, over a million people live on these shores. Geologists have discovered evidence of four previous prehistoric tsunamis, warning that this Alpine tragedy remains a recurring threat.
angle: A landlocked tsunami in the Swiss Alps reached 42 feet high and scaled the city walls of Geneva in 563 AD.

claims.claim: The Tauredunum event occurred in 563 AD.

evidence.quote: The Tauredunum event (German: Tauredunum-Ereignis) of 563 AD was a tsunami on Lake Geneva
In 563 A.D., a rock fall took place in the mountains more than 45 miles (70 kilometers) from Geneva

claims.claim: The disaster was recorded by contemporary chroniclers Gregory of Tours and Marius of Avenches.

evidence.quote: according to two historical accounts — one from St. Gregory of Tours, the other from Marius, bishop of Avenches.
The flooding in AD 563 was described by contemporary authors Gregory of Tours and Marius of Avenches

claims.claim: The event was triggered by a mountainside collapse at a place called Tauredunum.

evidence.quote: the disaster was caused by the collapse of a mountainside at a place called Tauredunum at the eastern end of Lake Geneva.
the disaster was caused by the collapse of a mountainside at a place called Tauredunum at the eastern end of Lake Geneva.

claims.claim: The landslide occurred where the River Rhone enters Lake Geneva.

evidence.quote: The rock fall, known as the Tauredunum event after a nearby fort, brought down boulders near where the Rhone River enters Lake Geneva.
a massive rock fall – probably from the Le Grammont mountain close to where the Rhône flows into lake at its eastern end – caused part of the river delta to collapse

claims.claim: The rock fall triggered an underwater collapse of sediment at the Rhone delta.

evidence.quote: the Tauredunum landslide triggered the collapse of sediments that had accumulated at the point where the River Rhône flows into Lake Geneva.
The researchers guess that the rock fall’s impact on soft sediments near the lakeshore caused part of the delta to collapse, which triggered a tsunami.

claims.claim: The wave reached Lausanne within 15 minutes of the event.

evidence.quote: It would have struck Lausanne within only 15 minutes, where it would have been about 13 metres (43 ft) high
massive tsunami about 42 feet high when it reached Lausanne in about 15 minutes.

claims.claim: The tsunami reached Geneva approximately 70 minutes after the initial impact.

evidence.quote: producing a tsunami up to 16 metres (52 ft) high that reached Geneva within about 70 minutes.
a wave about 25 feet high traveling at around 45 miles per hour could have reached Geneva approximately 70 minutes following the original impact.

claims.claim: The tsunami destroyed the bridge and mills in Geneva.

evidence.quote: demolished the Geneva bridge and mills
destroyed a bridge and mills in Geneva

claims.claim: The wave surged over the city walls of Geneva.

evidence.quote: it washed over the city walls and killed many of the inhabitants.
even crashed over the city walls of Geneva, killing several people inside.

claims.claim: Researchers found a sediment deposit approximately 6 miles long and 3 miles wide on the lake bed.

evidence.quote: They found sediment deposits more than 6 miles long and 3 miles wide.
They discovered a “tongue” of material about 6 miles long, 3 miles wide and 16 feet deep on average

claims.claim: Dating of organic materials in the lake sediment core indicated a date between 381 and 612 AD.

evidence.quote: Biological material found in the turbidite enabled it to be dated to between 381 and 612
organic materials found in a core of the tongue indicate it was formed between AD 381 and 612.

claims.claim: Over one million people currently live along the shores of Lake Geneva.

evidence.quote: over a million people now live along the lake's shores.
endangering the 1 million people who live in low-lying areas along the shore.

disputed: The exact location of the Tauredunum fort and the landslide has been debated for centuries, with sites like Saint-Maurice and Saint-Gingolph suggested before modern researchers identified Le Grammont.
Early theories suggested the wave was caused by a dam burst on the Rhone, but modern seismic data favors a sediment collapse mechanism.
Wave height estimates at Geneva vary slightly between 25 feet, 26 feet, and 28 feet depending on the source simulation.
